answer:
HEADLINE ANSWER
In the Psychology replication corpus (project "rpp", the 97-pair Reproducibility Project), junior professors — the Assistant-Professor rank — led 10 of the 35 successful replications: 10/35 = 28.6% (Wilson 95% CI 16.3–45.1%).

Reproducible filter chain (single file, no join): file A `meta-regression_study_data_heterogeneity_in_replication_projects.csv` → project == 'rpp' (n=97 rows, one row per original-study/replication pair, lab_id empty) → replicated == 1 (n=35) → numerator = count of seniority.r == 'Assistant Professor' = 10. Denominators are complete (0 missing seniority.r and 0 missing replicated inside rpp), so no imputation was used.

HYPOTHESIS (the submitted natural-language claim)
"About 29% (10/35) of the replications that succeeded in the Psychology replication project (rpp) were led by a junior professor (Assistant Professor) as most senior author, versus 23.7% (23/97) of all attempted rpp pairs — i.e. junior-led teams were numerically over-represented among successful replications but not reliably so (Fisher exact OR = 1.51, p = 0.46). The figure is a study-level share of most-senior-author rank in this corpus, not a share of individual authors and not an estimate of junior-professor prevalence in psychology generally."

SENSITIVITY TABLE (full grid in analysis/results/sensitivity_table.csv; 36 rows)
Definition / scenario                                        numerator/denominator   %
PRIMARY  rpp, replicated==1, pairs, seniority.r, J1=AsstProf        10 / 35        28.6  [16.3, 45.1]
co-primary  rpp, all attempted pairs, seniority.r, J1               23 / 97        23.7  [16.4, 33.1]
  contrast  rpp, replicated==0, seniority.r, J1                     13 / 62        21.0  [12.7, 32.6]
J2 = {AsstProf, Assistant}, replicated==1                           16 / 35        45.7  [30.5, 61.8]
J3 = below full Prof, replicated==1                                 23 / 35        65.7  [49.2, 79.2]
seniority.o, J1, replicated==1                                       0 / 35         0.0  (DEGENERATE, see below)
seniority.o, J3, replicated==1                                       4 / 35        11.4   [4.5, 26.0]
drop==False only, replicated==1, J1                                 10 / 31        32.3  [18.6, 49.9]
drop==False only, all attempted, J1                                 22 / 90        24.4  [16.7, 34.2]
unique-original-study, replicated==1, J1                            10 / 34        29.4  [16.8, 46.2]
unique-original-study, all attempted, J1                            23 / 94        24.5  [16.9, 34.0]
all psychology projects (rpp+ml1+ml3, aggregated==True only),
   replicated==1, J1                                                10 / 52        19.2  [10.8, 31.9]
all psychology projects, all attempted, J1                          23 / 123       18.7  [12.8, 26.5]
Choice of junior definition moves the answer far more than choice of denominator: J1 28.6% → J2 45.7% → J3 65.7%; switching denominator (35 → 97) moves it only ~5 points; drop flag ~+3.7 points; pair vs unique study ~+0.8 points. The ml-inclusive variant is NOT comparable to the headline: seniority.r is 'Professor' for all 26 ml1/ml3 aggregated studies (consortium-wide most senior author), so it dilutes the junior share mechanically rather than measuring it.

seniority.o diagnostic (reported, not buried): among the 35 successful rpp replications the original papers' most senior authors were Professor 30 (85.7%), Associate Professor 4 (11.4%), Researcher 1 (2.9%), and ZERO Assistant/Assistant Professor. The seniority.o-based junior-professor proportion is therefore 0% by construction, which is why the replication-side field is the only usable one. That seniority.r is the replication-side rank (rather than the "original paper" wording in datasets.json) is my INFERENCE from the crosstab — .o and .r vary independently inside rpp (e.g. Professor-original → Assistant-original-rank in 13 pairs) — and is not confirmed metadata.

WHAT DRIVES THE NUMBER (10 pairs listed in analysis/results/headline_junior_pairs.csv)
The 10 junior-led successes are Assistant-Professor-led replications of mostly senior-authored originals (9 of 10 originals led by a full Professor, 1 by an Associate Professor); 6 cognitive / 4 social; original journals JEPLMC 4, Psychological Science 4, JPSP 2 (rpp draws on only these three journals); 4 of them replicate with very large effects (p < 1e-3, e.g. rpp.113 prescribed optimism r=.76, rpp.142 anger regulation r=.61); median relative_es 0.94 vs 1.00 for the other 25 successful replications. None carry drop == True, which is why excluding drop-flagged rows leaves the numerator at 10 and only shrinks the denominator to 31. Context from the full rank mix: junior ranks are common in rpp replications overall (AsstProf 23.7%, Assistant 15.5%, Associate 24.7%, Professor 19.6%, Researcher 16.5% of the 97 attempted), so the headline mainly reflects who staffed replication teams in this corpus, not that junior-led teams uniquely succeed (junior share 28.6% among successes vs 21.0% among failures, OR 1.51, p = 0.46).

REQUIRED CAVEAT (one line)
No author-level roster exists in either file, so this is a study-level proportion of "most senior author rank" per replication pair — not a share of individual authors; a junior professor leading a large team counts once, and co-authors' ranks are invisible.

LIMIT OF THE CLAIM + DATA QUALITY
Descriptive share within this corpus only (97 rpp pairs, 35 successes, 3 source journals, 2015 OSC-style RPP design); not a prevalence estimate for psychology. All 12 pre-registered checks passed (analysis/results/data_quality_checks.csv): rpp has exactly one row per pair (0 lab_id rows, 97 unique ids); seniority/replicated 100% complete in rpp; seniority strings are exactly the 5 canonical levels with no case/whitespace variants; the replicated flag is reproducible from p_value.r <= .05 & same sign (100% on the 94 pairs with complete data, 3 lack effect_size.r); the 3 duplicated original studies (rpp.49/50, rpp.58/59, rpp.148/149) were kept as separate pairs in the primary run and handled by first-id deduplication in the unique-study variant (rpp.58 vs rpp.59 disagree on both rank and outcome, so deduplication discards real information); 7 provider drop==True rows counted and reported separately; ml1/ml3 lab rows (786) were never used for study-level figures — only the 26 aggregated == True rows.

COVERAGE GAP (flagged, not imputed): file B carries no seniority or author field and cannot inform the numerator. Its 73 "Psychology" rows name-match only 68 of the 97 rpp pairs, leaving 29 rpp pairs with no counterpart and 1 duplicated study label; on the matched pairs the two files' replication outcomes agree 100% (recomputing pr <= .05 & same sign in file B), so the gap looks like an undocumented subset selection in file B rather than a conflict, and I have not modelled it.

payload.hypothesis: About 29% (10 of 35) of the replications that succeeded in the Psychology replication project (project == 'rpp') were led by a junior professor (Assistant Professor) as most senior author, compared with 23.7% (23/97) of all attempted rpp pairs; junior-led replications were numerically more likely to succeed (28.6% of successes vs 21.0% of failures) but the association is not statistically reliable (Fisher exact OR = 1.51, p = 0.46). Broader readings of 'junior' raise the share to 45.7% (adding 'Assistant') or 65.7% (anything below full Professor), while an original-side reading (seniority.o) is 0% by construction.
payload.workflow: 1) Inspected both staged CSVs and diagnosed the mixed row units (ml1/ml3 = 786 lab rows + 26 aggregated study rows; rpp/ee = one row per original-study/replication pair). 2) Built the frame from file A only: project == 'rpp' (97 pairs, Psychology per datasets.json coding); file B used only as a non-authoritative cross-check (no seniority field). 3) Primary statistic: among rpp pairs with replicated == 1 (n=35), share with seniority.r == 'Assistant Professor' = 10/35 = 28.57% (Wilson 95% CI 16.3-45.1). 4) Ran a 36-cell sensitivity grid over junior definition (AsstProf / +Assistant / below full Professor), seniority field (.r vs degenerate .o), denominator (replicated==1 vs all 97, plus replicated==0 contrast), provider drop flag, pair-level vs unique-original-study, and an 'all psychology projects' variant using aggregated == True rows only (never lab rows). 5) Characterised drivers: listed the 10 junior-led successes with their original-paper journal, discipline, original lead rank, replication p-value/effect and relative_es; ran a Fisher exact test for junior rank x replication success. 6) Passed 12 data-quality checks (unit integrity, completeness, category hygiene, reproducibility of the replicated flag, duplicate original studies, drop flag, ml aggregation guard) and flagged the 29-of-97 undocumented rpp coverage gap relative to file B without imputation. Outputs: analysis/results/{report.txt, sensitivity_table.csv, headline_junior_pairs.csv, data_quality_checks.csv, fileB_crosscheck_matches.csv}.

headline.filter_chain: file A -> project == 'rpp' -> replicated == 1 -> seniority.r == 'Assistant Professor'

payload.caveat: Study-level proportion of most-senior-author rank per replication pair (no author-level roster exists), descriptive of this rpp corpus only.
limitations: 'junior professor' is not an explicit category in the data; estimate ranges 28.6% (Assistant Professor) to 65.7% (below full Professor)
seniority field choice is decisive: seniority.o yields 0% inside rpp (no junior-professorial original lead authors exist there)
n=35 denominator gives a wide 95% CI (16.3-45.1%)
seniority.r = replication-side rank is an inference from the crosstab, not confirmed metadata
29 of 97 rpp pairs have no counterpart in file B (undocumented coverage gap, not imputed); rpp covers only 3 journals
